Add the powdered sugar and cocoa powder and whisk until smooth. Add the flour and stir with a spatula just until no dry streaks remain. Fold in the roughly chopped chocolate just until evenly distributed, being careful not to overmix.
Lightly grease an 8” (20cm) baking pan with nonstick cooking spray. Cut a sheet of parchment paper slightly narrower than the pan but long enough to cover the bottom and two opposite sides, leaving a few inches of overhang on each side. Press the parchment into the greased pan. The overhanging parchment will act as handles for lifting the brownies from the pan after baking.
Transfer the batter to the prepared pan and spread it into an even layer, making sure to work the batter into the corners. Bake for 20–25 minutes, or until the edges are set and the center is still slightly soft. A toothpick inserted into the center should come out with a few moist crumbs attached, but no wet batter.
Let the brownies cool completely in the pan. Using the parchment sling, lift them from the pan and transfer them to a cutting board. Slice into 9 even squares, serve, and enjoy!

a8f89a027473b48d115a4de4ac9b00bced6811d1.title: The Perfect Breakfast Burrito
a8f89a027473b48d115a4de4ac9b00bced6811d1.author: Joshua Weissman
a8f89a027473b48d115a4de4ac9b00bced6811d1.ingredients:
1 cup (140g) garlic cloves, peeled
2 cups (480mL) neutral oil (vegetable, avocado, etc.)
8 jalapeños, blistered and peeled
2 large egg yolks
3 limes (juice of all, zest of 1)
½ bunch fresh cilantro
Reserved confit garlic from above
Kosher salt, to taste
Water, to loosen
1¾ cups (420mL) reserved garlic oil, or as needed
4 guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
2 ancho chiles, stemmed and seeded
4 chiles de arbol, stemmed and seeded
¼ tsp (1g) ground cinnamon
½ tsp (2g) onion powder
1 tsp (2g) ground coriander
2 tsp (8g) ground cumin
1 Tbsp + 1 tsp (13g) kosher salt
2 Tbsp (30mL) white distilled vinegar
2 cloves garlic
1½ lbs (680g) fatty ground pork
Neutral oil, for frying
Neutral oil, for frying
6 frozen McDonald’s-style hash browns
Kosher salt, to taste
2½ Tbsp (35g) unsalted butter
12 large eggs
Kosher salt, to taste
3 avocados, cut into 1” (2.5cm) slices
Flaky salt, to taste
Lime juice, to taste
6 large flour tortillas
2 cups (400g) Oaxaca cheese, shredded
a8f89a027473b48d115a4de4ac9b00bced6811d1.instructions:
Add the garlic and oil to a small saucepot. Set over medium-low heat and cook, stirring occasionally, until the garlic is completely tender and lightly golden brown, about 10–15 minutes. Keep the heat gentle to avoid browning the garlic too quickly.
Strain the garlic from the oil through a fine-mesh strainer. Reserve both the garlic and oil separately and let cool to room temperature.
Char the jalapeños on all sides over an open flame or under the broiler until the skins are completely blackened.
Transfer the jalapeños to a bowl and cover tightly with plastic wrap. Let steam for about 5 minutes to soften the peppers and loosen their skins. Peel away the charred skin using a damp paper towel. Remove and discard the stems.
Add the jalapeños to a blender along with the egg yolks, lime juice, lime zest, reserved confit garlic, cilantro, and a generous pinch of salt. Blend on medium until smooth, adding a small splash of water only if necessary to get the mixture moving.
Increase the speed to medium-high and slowly stream in the reserved garlic oil until the sauce is thick, smooth, and emulsified. You may not need all of the oil depending on your desired consistency. Taste and adjust with salt and additional lime juice as necessary. Refrigerate until ready to serve.
Bring a small pot of water to a boil. Add the guajillo, ancho, and árbol chiles, cover, and reduce the heat to low. Simmer until the chiles are softened and pliable, about 3–5 minutes. Remove the chiles, reserving ½ cup (120mL) of the soaking liquid.
Add the rehydrated chiles to a blender along with the cinnamon, onion powder, coriander, cumin, salt, garlic, and vinegar. Blend on high, adding the reserved chile water a splash at a time as needed, until the mixture forms a smooth purée. Let cool completely to room temperature.
Add the ground pork and chile purée to a large mixing bowl. Using gloved hands, mix until evenly incorporated and slightly tacky. Cover and marinate for a minimum of 2 hours, ideally overnight.
Lightly coat the bottom of a large skillet with neutral oil and set over medium-high heat. Once hot, add the chorizo and press it into an even layer. Leave undisturbed to sear for 2–3 minutes.
Use a potato masher or wooden spoon to break the pork into small crumbles. Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until cooked through and deeply caramelized in spots, about 5–8 minutes. Taste and adjust with salt as necessary. Remove from the heat and keep warm for assembly.
Heat at least 2” (5cm) of neutral oil in a Dutch oven or heavy-bottomed pot to 350°F (177°C).
Working in batches as necessary, deep-fry the frozen hash browns according to package directions, or until golden brown and crispy, about 3–5 minutes.
Transfer to a wire rack set over a baking sheet and immediately season to taste with salt. Cut each hash brown in half crosswise for assembly.
Crack the eggs into a large mixing bowl and whisk until completely homogeneous.
Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium heat. Add the butter and swirl until melted and foamy but not browned. Add the eggs and season to taste with salt.
Using a rubber spatula, constantly stir and fold the eggs, scraping along the bottom and sides of the skillet. Move the skillet on and off the heat as necessary to control the temperature and develop small, tender curds.
Continue cooking until the eggs are softly set but no longer runny; they should be slightly softer than you ultimately want them since they’ll continue cooking during assembly and toasting. Remove from the heat.
Season the avocado slices with flaky salt and lime juice to taste. Warm the flour tortillas until hot and pliable. Place one tortilla on a clean work surface.
Across the lower third of the tortilla, layer the chorizo, scrambled eggs, 2 hash brown halves, seasoned avocado, and Oaxaca cheese. Be careful not to overfill.
Fold the left and right sides of the tortilla inward over the filling, then tightly roll from the bottom up to form a burrito. Repeat with the remaining tortillas and filling.
Heat a large skillet over medium heat. Place each burrito seam-side down and toast until golden brown, about 1–2 minutes. Rotate and continue toasting until golden and crisp on all sides and the cheese is melted.
Slice each burrito in half, serve with the jalapeño sauce, and enjoy!

9066c6fdf05d270605e0338174db589c7b07a5b5.title: Rissoles with Curry Sauce
9066c6fdf05d270605e0338174db589c7b07a5b5.text: This was a staple dinner option for Katelyn when she was growing up. Juicy, plump beef rissoles served with a rich curry sauce, with some mashed potatoes and green beans on the side. You don’t need to make it with beef, you can swap the protein for chicken, lamb or turkey. I think these rissoles have plenty of flavour but the curry sauce just takes it to another level. If the kids don’t like the curry sauce, you can always add the classic tomato sauce on the side (I won’t be offended). The prep and cooking time will only take you 40 minutes and you can steam some veggies, prep a salad, or make some mashed potatoes at the same time.Ingredient NotesMince - I like to use 80/20 beef mince, so 80 meat 20% fat to ensure it’s nice and juicy once cooked. You can go for a leaner mince but it may not be as juicy. You can also use chicken, pork, lamb or turkey mince. Breadcrumbs - You want to buy fine, dried breadcrumbs for this recipe as they will hydrate well in the milk and bind properly to the mince. Peanut oil - for this recipe, I like to use a neutral flavoured oil so you get the full flavour of the beef in the rissoles. Neutral flavoured oils include peanut, canola or vegetable oil. If you would prefer olive oil, that’s fine - it will still taste good. Maggi seasoning - this is to boost the depth of flavour and add extra salty and umami flavours. It is quite strong so you don’t need too much. If you don’t have it, you can swap out for light soy sauce instead, it won’t be the same but it will be close. Carrot & Zucchini - Make sure you squeeze out as much liquid as possible before adding to the rissole mixture. You’ll get enough moisture from the mince, and any extra may cause the rissoles to break or start to steam in the pan so you’ll lose the colour and crust. Tools﻿Here’s some key equipment you’ll need for this cook.Standing grater - For the carrots, zucchini and onion. Mixing bowls - You’ll need two large (for the grated veg and one for the rissole mixture) and one small mixing (for the breadcrumb mixture) bowl. Trays - One to line your rissoles on before cooking and then another with a rack for one they’re cooked. Small/medium saucepan - I use a small/medium stainless steel saucepan or saucier (around 20cm/ 7.8 inches), to cook the curry sauce in. Large casserole dish - This is to cook your rissoles in. I’ve used a enamelled cast iron casserole dish but you can also use a large cast iron or carbon steel frying pan. Chefs knife, chopping board, tongs, wooden spoon and whisk
9066c6fdf05d270605e0338174db589c7b07a5b5.author: Andy
9066c6fdf05d270605e0338174db589c7b07a5b5.ingredients:
1 carrot
1 zucchini
sea salt and black pepper, to season
120g dried breadcrumbs
60ml (¼ cup) milk
500g beef mince
1 brown onion
20ml (1 tbsp) Worcestershire sauce
1 tsp Maggi seasoning
peanut oil (or other neutral flavoured oil), for frying
mashed potato and steamed broccolini, to serve
40g butter
1 brown onion
1 thumb-size piece fresh ginger
3 cloves garlic
20g plain flour
2 tsp tomato paste (tomato puree)
1½ tbsp curry powder
250ml (1 cup) chicken stock
1 tsp honey
9066c6fdf05d270605e0338174db589c7b07a5b5.instructions:
Grate the carrot and zucchini and combine in another large bowl. Season with salt and mix well, then set aside for 20 minutes.
Combine the breadcrumbs and milk in a large bowl and mix well. Set aside to soak for 10 minutes.
Grate the onion and add to the breadcrumbs mixture, along with the beef mince, Worcestershire sauce, Maggi seasoning, and season with salt and pepper.
Squeeze all the excess liquid from the carrot and zucchini mixture, then add to the meat mixture. Mix well, then portion into 60g patties, place on a large tray and gently flatten.
Finely dice the onion (or you could grate it) and finely grate the ginger and garlic.
Melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the onions, season with some salt and cook for 2-3 minutes, stirring, until softened.
Add the ginger and garlic and stir through, then sprinkle over the flour. Cook for 1-2 minutes to cook the flour out, stirring constantly.
Add the tomato paste and mix through well, then add the curry powder and cook for 1 minute to toast the powder.
Gradually whisk in chicken stock until smooth and bring to a simmer. Stir in the honey and season to taste. Reduce the heat to low and let simmer while you cook the rissoles.
Heat enough peanut oil in a large frying pan to cover the base of the pan, over medium-high heat.
Cook the rissoles, in batches, for 9-10 minutes, turning when browned well on each side. Transfer to a tray and repeat with the next batch.
Serve the rissoles on a bed of mashed potato, with some steamed broccolini on the side. Spoon over the curry sauce and serve.

b840369baa36ae656a2c08192e1d1aacf883e845.title: Cajun Chicken Alfredo
b840369baa36ae656a2c08192e1d1aacf883e845.text: This one takes me back to working in cafes in Auckland, the classic cajun chicken alfredo. If you're wanting a comforting pasta dish that's nice and creamy, well this is your recipe! It's an Americanised pasta dish that use a heavy cream to thicken the sauce and a cajun spice blend to season it. It's great for a quick, hearty meal during the week as it doesn't have too many ingredients and it's very quick to make. This recipe is just for one person, but you can easily scale up if you're making it for 2 or more people. Ingredient NotesCajun spice blend: Every brand is slightly different and they often have a fair bit of salt in them, so make sure you taste the dish with the seasoning in it before adding the additional salt. Chicken breast: Cut your chicken breasts into strips around the same thickness as the zuchinni so they cook at the same rate. Breast is known to dry out fast, so we'll just get it brown on the outside before adding the cream in to continue cooking. Parmesan: I recommend buying a block and grating it yourself. I'm not a fan of pre-grated parmesan as it's coated in anti-caking agents to stop it melting and doesn't give the same result. EquipmentMedium pot (for boiling pasta) Medium saucier (or frying pan) Chef’s knife Chopping board Fine grater Tongs
b840369baa36ae656a2c08192e1d1aacf883e845.author: Andy
b840369baa36ae656a2c08192e1d1aacf883e845.ingredients:
2 zucchini (courgettes)
1 chicken breast, boneless, skinless
1 tbsp olive oil
1 ½ tsp Cajun spice blend
100g (3.5 oz) dried fettuccine pasta
100ml (3.3 fl oz) thickened/heavy cream
30g (1 oz) Parmesan cheese
salt to taste
b840369baa36ae656a2c08192e1d1aacf883e845.instructions:
Place a medium pot of lightly salted water on high heat to boil.
Slice the zucchini in half lengthwise, then slice on an angle about 1cm thick.
Slice the chicken into strips, a similar thickness to the courgettes.
Preheat a medium saucier on high heat with the oil. Once the oil is hot, add the chicken, ¼ tsp salt, Cajun seasoning and courgettes. Stir to combine.
Place the pasta into the boiling water for 8-12 minutes (depending on the brand you’re using) until al dente.
Once the chicken becomes golden brown and the courgettes begin to sweat, turn the heat down to medium and add the cream. As the cream reduces, the chicken will finish cooking. Continue simmering for 6-7 minutes until the chicken is cooked through, the cream has thickened and become glossy. Taste and adjust the seasoning until you’re happy with the flavour. Turn the heat down to low until the pasta is ready.
Once the pasta is cooked, use tongs to remove the pasta from the boiling water and add to the chicken. Finely grate the Parmesan cheese and toss through the sauce to combine, then plate.

2affc23eebb92251137d98379cf87ef5c5ba7028.title: Creamy Chicken Pie
2affc23eebb92251137d98379cf87ef5c5ba7028.text: I love a good chicken pie. It’s not something I make all that often but when I do it’s just so moreish and I remember how good it is. I like to make it if I have a few friends coming round for a casual dinner and we want something warming. I can do all the prep and most of the cooking before they arrive. I’ll also put together an easy leaf salad to go with it. Ingredient NotesChicken thighs: You want thighs for this recipe, not breast. As this has a long cook time, we need a cut that will stay juicy and tender like the thigh. Cut it into 2cm cubes so it cooks evenly and is easy to chew when you're eating your pie. Puff and shortcrust pastry: We're using both for this recipe, the shortcrust will line the base and the walls as it's more sturdy and the puff will go on top for a crisp, flakey pie top. Keep both cold right up until you're measuring out your pie pieces. It's much easier to work when it's cold. EquipmentChopping board Chef’s knife Large rondeau or pot Small bowl Pastry brush 22cm (9-inch) springform cake tin SpatulaWhisk or forkParchment paper
2affc23eebb92251137d98379cf87ef5c5ba7028.author: Andy
2affc23eebb92251137d98379cf87ef5c5ba7028.ingredients:
2 brown onions
2 carrots
3 celery sticks
6 cloves garlic, peeled
6 sprigs thyme
½ bunch dill
1kg (2.2 lbs) chicken thighs, boneless and skinless
50g (3.5 tbsp) unsalted butter
100g (¾ cup) plain flour
50ml (3 tbsp) olive oil
sea salt, to taste
black and white pepper to taste
500ml (2 cups) chicken stock
3 tsp dijon mustard
1 chicken bouillon stock cube
240ml (1 cup) whole milk
300g (2 cups) frozen peas
375g frozen puff pastry sheet, thawed
2 x 375g frozen short crust pastry sheets, thawed
spray oil
1 egg
2affc23eebb92251137d98379cf87ef5c5ba7028.instructions:
Peel the onion, slice in half and remove the core. Slice the onion into a rough 1cm dice.
Top and tail, then peel and dice the carrot a similar size to the onion. Dice the celery the same size.
Crush and roughly dice the garlic. Set all vegetables aside and keep separate.
If you’re using young, soft thyme, finely slice. If the stem is hard, pick off the leaves before finely slicing.
Finely slice the dill.
Prepare the chicken by slicing it into 2cm cubes then set aside.
Preheat a large rondeau or large pot over medium heat. Add the butter and stir until melted. Add the flour and continue stirring for 1-2 minutes until the flour absorbs the fat and begins to smell like unsweetened cookies. Remove the roux, cover and transfer to the fridge for later.
Wipe out the pot you used to make the roux and add the olive oil.
Sweat the onion in the oil for two minutes, then add the carrot and celery. Continue sweating until the vegetables just begin to soften.
Turn the heat up to high then add the chicken. Stir through with ½ tsp of salt and 6-7 cracks of black pepper. Continue cooking and stirring for 5-6 minutes until the outside of the chicken turns white (don’t worry if it’s not cooked all the way through yet).
Add the thyme and garlic and stir through for 1 minute.
Add the chicken stock, dijon mustard and chicken stock cube. Bring to a simmer, then incorporate in the roux from earlier. Stir until the roux has been fully absorbed into the sauce.
Add the milk and stir until the sauce is homogeneous.
Continue cooking for 3-4 minutes until you are left with a smooth, glossy thick sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with white pepper and salt if needed.
Stir through the frozen peas and chopped dill. Transfer the mixture to a large, flat tray. Place in the fridge for 1-2 hours or until cool all the way through.
Place a sheet of puff pastry under the cake tin. Cut around the circumference of the tin. This sheet of pastry will be used for the top of the pie. Place the sheet of pastry, with parchment paper underneath, into the freezer for ½ hour maximum to firm up.
Using a sheet of shortcrust pastry, repeat the step above by cutting the same size disc. Set aside.
Lay a fresh piece of shortcrust pastry on a board. Stand the cake tin on its side and place over the pastry to mark the depth of the cake tin on the pastry. Cut out 2-3 strips of pastry to use as the walls of the pie.
Lightly grease the inside of the cake tin with spray oil.
Use the pastry strips you cut to line the inside of the tin. Press the pastry into the sides firmly with your fingers and crimp the ends where the sheets meet. If the pastry isn’t sticking you can use a light brush of egg wash to help them stick.
Insert the disk of shortcrust pastry into the base. Use your index finger to join the sides of the pastry with the base.
Transfer the lined cake tin into the freezer to firm up for 10 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F).
Remove the filling from the fridge and the cake tin from the freezer. Spoon the filling into the cake tin and push it down with the back of a spoon to release any air bubbles. Make sure there’s at least a 1cm gap between the top of the filling and the top of the cake tin. If you have excess filling, save it for another use instead of packing it all into the tin.
In a small bowl, whisk the egg.
Use a pastry brush to lightly brush the inside of the exposed pastry.
Remove the sheet of firm puff pastry from the freezer. If the pastry is frozen, not firm, then leave it on the bench to defrost for a few minutes.
Place the disk of puff pastry on top of the pie, then crimp the exposed shortcrust pastry over the top to help seal in the lid.
Cut a small cross in the very center of the lid, cutting right through the pastry. This acts as a vent to allow steam to escape as the pie bakes.
Lightly brush the top of the pie with the beaten egg and season with a light pinch of flaky salt.
Place the pie in the oven for 45-50 minutes until the pastry is golden brown and puffed.
Rest the pie for 10-15 minutes before popping it out of the cake tin. Serve and enjoy.

cee359afa3a47212a0dd97575be6054775329bfd.title: Ground Lamb Curry For One (Keema)
cee359afa3a47212a0dd97575be6054775329bfd.text: Lamb Keema is a really simple curry to make. So if you're new to cooking, or you want something simple and quick for dinner, give this one a try. This recipe is a dialled back, weeknight friendly adaptation of the classic which often calls for potatoes and whole spices. If you want the classic version, check it out here. This recipe is designed to be fast, full of flavour and absolutely delicious. It's just lamb mince, some spices, garlic and ginger, tinned tomatoes and some peas, served over rice. If you're not a fan of lamb, you can switch it for beef. And feel free to add some extra veg if you like. Ingredient NotesLamb mince: It generally has more fat than beef mince and you want that extra fat to help toast all the spices you're going to add. You can also use beef, chicken turkey or pork mince for this dish, just add some extra oil as they won't have as much fat as the lamb. Ground spices: This uses my four favourite spices; garam masala, ground chilli, ground cumin and ground coriander. If you like some extra heat, add more ground chilli in. EquipmentChef’s knife Chopping board Fine grater Medium saucier or saucepan Wooden spatula Bench scraper (optional)
cee359afa3a47212a0dd97575be6054775329bfd.author: Andy
cee359afa3a47212a0dd97575be6054775329bfd.ingredients:
1 brown onion
5 cloves garlic
1 thumb-sized piece of ginger
1 tbsp peanut (or neutral flavoured) oil
200g (7 oz) lamb mince
½ tsp garam masala
¼ tsp ground chilli
½ tsp ground cumin
½ tbsp ground coriander
400g (14.5 oz) tinned crushed tomatoes
70g peas (fresh or frozen)
salt to taste
1 cup steamed rice to serve
cee359afa3a47212a0dd97575be6054775329bfd.instructions:
Peel and finely dice the onion then set aside.
Peel the ginger and garlic, then finely grate both and set aside.
Place a medium saucier or saucepan over high heat. Add the oil and wait for it to heat. Add in the diced onion with ¼ tsp salt and sweat for 2 minutes, stirring often until the onions become translucent.
Add in the lamb mince, grated ginger, garlic and ground spices. Stir and sear until the spices become fragrant and the mince has lightly browned.
Add in the tinned tomatoes with a splash (50ml) of water. Stir and reduce the heat to a medium simmer for 8 minutes.
Add in the peas, if using fresh peas, cook for 4 minutes until soft. If the peas are pre-frozen, they take just 2 minutes to heat through.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Serve over steamed rice and enjoy.

c3ea8f647427fbb50a7a9dc862893a82a4cf3017.title: Bacon and Kimchi Fried Rice
c3ea8f647427fbb50a7a9dc862893a82a4cf3017.text: Fried rice is a classic leftovers dish, once that you can tweak to your liking and use what you have in the fridge. One of my favourite combinations is the kimchi fried rice with bacon. Kimchi just adds a great sour and spicy note to the dish and the bacon brings a nice fatty richness to it. I use both kimchi and kimchi juice, so make sure you don't discard the juice!Do I need day old rice? Ideally you have cold rice in your fridge but if you don't, I've heard the microwave rice packets also work well for fried rice.We're going to cook this in a wok and it only takes about 4 minutes to cook, so make sure all your prep is done before you start throwing things in the wok. Ingredient NotesBacon or speck: I like to use a thick cut so you can get 1cm cubes out of it. If pork isn’t your thing, you can easily swap the bacon for prawns or chunks of white fish. Just slice them into bite sized pieces before cooking. Kimchi: Squeeze your kimchi over a bowl so you get most of the moisture out and keep the juice aside. Slice the kimchi into strips so it's easier to eat in your fried rice. Jasmine rice: Ideally you have day old, cold rice in your fridge. Why? It loses it's surface moisture so the grains stay seperate in the wok instead of clumping together. Packet microwave also works for the same reason. If you only have fresh rice, spread it on a tray and leave it in the fridge for an hour. EquipmentWok Chopping board Chef’s knife Flat wooden spatula or wok turnerSmall bowlLarge plate
c3ea8f647427fbb50a7a9dc862893a82a4cf3017.author: Andy
c3ea8f647427fbb50a7a9dc862893a82a4cf3017.ingredients:
90g (3.2 oz) thick cut bacon or speck
1 bunch choy sum
80g (2.8 oz) kimchi
1 clove garlic
3 tbsp peanut oil (or neutral flavoured oil)
1 cup (200g / 7 oz) pre-cooked jasmine rice (day old or cooked packet rice works well)
1 tsp oyster sauce
½ tsp sesame oil
1 egg
c3ea8f647427fbb50a7a9dc862893a82a4cf3017.instructions:
Slice the thick cut bacon or speck into cubes about 1cm x 1cm, then set aside.
Wash the choy sum then slice off the base at the bottom of the stem. Slice the stalks 2-3cm long. When you get to the green leaves, slice them into thinner ribbons about 1cm thick. Keep the two parts separate.
Squeeze the kimchi but reserve the juice for later. Place the drained kimchi on your board and roughly slice into strips.
Peel the garlic clove then crush and finely chop.
Place a wok over high heat. To test if your wok is hot enough, add a few drops of water into the centre. If the water evaporates instantly or dances around like pearls, it’s ready to go. Make sure the wok is fully dry, before adding 1 tbsp of peanut oil. Once the oil just starts to smoke, add in the bacon and stir for 10-20 seconds. Add the kimchi and continue frying for a further 30 seconds.
Add in the garlic and stalks of the choy sum, then the rice. Before stirring, drizzle 1 tbsp of peanut oil directly over the rice and leave it to warm through, this helps to prevent sticking.
Mix the ingredients together, then add in the juice from the kimchi, oyster sauce and the tops of the choy sum. Once the greens have wilted, finish the dish with the sesame oil.
Tip the fried rice onto a large plate and return the wok back to the heat.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp of peanut oil to the wok, then crack the egg into the centre. You want the whites to be crisp and fluffy while the yolk stays runny. Keep the wok moving to maintain an even heat source for the egg. Once cooked, place it on top of the fried rice dish and enjoy.

ca84f3c7d4b5f9e589fc839e489eb7a31451bde8.title: Chorizo & White Bean Skillet
ca84f3c7d4b5f9e589fc839e489eb7a31451bde8.text: If I've had a big week at work and need something easy to cook (and I'm cooking for myself), this is what you'll find me making. It's a dish you can have for breakfast, lunch or dinner and can swap the ingredients with different meat, veg or beans you have in your kitchen. I'm using chorizo in this recipe as it gives it a really nice flavour. The chorizo also gets a nice browning on it adding to the texture. We'll also use some white beans but you can also use butter or Cannellini beans.This one only take 10 minutes to cook and only uses one pan, and I usually eat it straight from the pan so there's even less dishes to clean up. Just make sure you put a trivet under the pan after taking it off the heat as it will be hot! Ingredient NotesChorizo: Try to find a good butcher that makes chorizo sausages in your area (I like them spicy). As the fat renders from the chorizo the aromatic spices permeate throughout and give the dish a foundation of flavour. You can also use other sausages like Italian or bratwurst, you may just want to add some smoked paprika and chilli to get some of the chorizo character in there. White beans: I like to use canned white beans (like Cannellini, Haricot, or Great Northern). I use these beans because they are creamy and mild with thin skins. When you add water and chicken stock powder, the starch from the beans lightly thickens the liquid. This creates a glossy, emulsified pan sauce that clings to the spinach and helps to enrich the dish. Chicken stock powder: We're using a powder in this recipe so we can control the amount of liquid without losing flavour. EquipmentSkillet or saute pan Chopping board Chef’s knife Wooden spatula
ca84f3c7d4b5f9e589fc839e489eb7a31451bde8.author: Andy
ca84f3c7d4b5f9e589fc839e489eb7a31451bde8.ingredients:
1 chorizo
½ tbsp olive oil
400g tin (14 oz) white beans
½ tsp chicken stock powder
1 handful, 60g (2 oz) baby spinach
1 egg
salt and pepper to taste
⅓ baguette
ca84f3c7d4b5f9e589fc839e489eb7a31451bde8.instructions:
Slice the chorizo in half lengthwise, then slice it into 1cm thick pieces.
Place a skillet or frying pan on high heat. Add the olive oil, then sauté the sliced chorizo in the pan for 3-4 minutes until the fat renders out and the chorizo becomes golden brown.
Drain the tinned beans then add them to the pan and stir to combine. The beans are pre-cooked, so you just want to warm them through at this stage. Add 50ml water and the chicken stock powder then bring to a simmer.
Once simmering, add 2-3 cracks of black pepper, ¼ tsp salt and the baby spinach. Create a well in the centre of the pan then crack in the egg. Season the yolk with a light sprinkle of salt and continue cooking until the whites have turned opaque.
Turn the element off, taste the beans for seasoning and adjust as needed.
Serve with a portion of baguette and enjoy.

2c0c3e1a88c3c61e99613d00ef231c573b2ea7c2.title: Prawn and Chickpea Curry
2c0c3e1a88c3c61e99613d00ef231c573b2ea7c2.text: Making dinner for one? This is my go to curry when I'm only cooking for myself and don't want to use too many ingredients or too much mess. Most of the ingredients I will already have in the pantry or fridge and anything I'm missing I can easily pick up from the grocer on the way home. This is a Thai style curry which has a coconut milk base with a red curry paste. Once we build the curry we'll add chickpeas, prawns, baby spinach and lime juice to finish. Ingredient NotesRed curry paste: This is a blend of red chills, lemongrass, galangal and a mix of spices. It's very aromatic and is what gives this curry so much flavour. You'll be able to pick it up in a grocer or Asian supermarket. Demerara sugar: It's a type of minimally processed, raw cane sugar. For this recipe the best alternative would be any raw sugar, otherwise palm sugar or standard white sugar work well. We don’t add sugar here for the curry to be sweet; you want to add just enough so that the sugar balances the acid and spice. Equipment Chopping board Chef’s knife Medium saucier or medium saucepan Wooden spatulaSieve or colanderMeasuring cup
2c0c3e1a88c3c61e99613d00ef231c573b2ea7c2.author: Andy
2c0c3e1a88c3c61e99613d00ef231c573b2ea7c2.ingredients:
1 shallot
2 garlic cloves, peeled
1 tbsp neutral flavoured oil (ie. peanut oil)
2 tbsp Maesri red curry paste
1 tin (400ml) coconut milk
1 tin (240g drained) chickpeas
12 frozen prawns, defrosted
1 tsp demerara sugar
1 lime, juice
1 tbsp fish sauce
1 handful (20g) baby spinach
sea salt to taste
2c0c3e1a88c3c61e99613d00ef231c573b2ea7c2.instructions:
Peel and finely slice the shallot. Crush and roughly chop the garlic.
Preheat a medium saucier over medium heat with the oil. Add the shallot and garlic with a ¼ tsp salt, sauté for 1 minute.
Add the curry paste and stir for a further 1 minute. Turn the heat up high and add ½ cup of the coconut milk to the saucier, continue stirring for 4-5 minutes. When you notice the fat from the coconut milk beginning to crack (or split), it’s ready.
Add the drained chickpeas, prawns, remaining coconut milk, and sugar. Bring to a simmer on medium heat for 4 minutes.
Once the prawns are fully cooked, add in the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary. Turn the heat off and fold the baby spinach through the sauce. Serve and enjoy!

677ab4f468970f9d2a25d30d280e0314397240eb.title: Bulgogi Burger
677ab4f468970f9d2a25d30d280e0314397240eb.text: Have you clicked on this recipe and are wondering what a bulgogi burger is? Well it's a blend of two great dishes. The first being a burger and the second a Korean bulgogi, which is thinly sliced beef that's marinated in soy, sesame, garlic and grated pear and then seared before serving with a range of sides like rice, grilled greens etc. This dish add all those delicious Bulgogi flavours to the burger patty before it's goes on the grill and then stack on a burger with lettuce, tomato, cheese and a kimchi mayonnaise.So if you're wanting to try a new burger, I would highly recommend giving this a try! Ingredient NotesBeef mince: For this recipe, we're going to use a 80/20 lean to fat ratio which gives us a nice amount of fat to hold the burger together and make it nice a juicy once it's been grilled. If you are grinding your own mince, I recommend going for a fine grind as it binds better and has a nicer texture than a coarse grind. Kimchi: You can use any Kimchi from the supermarket or Asian grocer, you just want an older/more sour kimchi to balance with the fat in the mayo. Be sure to drain it properly before mixing with the mayonnaise otherwise the brine with thin the mayo out too much. Honey: We're using honey to sweeten the beef in this recipe but the traditional bulgogi generally uses grated pear. If you would prefer to use pear, just use half and grate it. Equipment ListCharcoal or gas BBQ Burger flipper Large bowl Kitchen scales Parchment paper Flat tray Flat tray with a resting rack Fine grater Chopping board Chef’s knife
677ab4f468970f9d2a25d30d280e0314397240eb.author: Andy
677ab4f468970f9d2a25d30d280e0314397240eb.ingredients:
1kg 80/20 (lean meat to fat ratio) beef mince
1/2 white onion
8 cloves garlic
1 ½ tbsp soy sauce
1 tbsp sesame oil
1 ½ tbsp runny honey
½ lettuce (butter or iceberg)
2 tomatoes
8 slices sliced cheddar cheese
80g (½ cup) kimchi
60g (¼ cup) mayonnaise
4 sesame seed burger buns.
Salt to taste
677ab4f468970f9d2a25d30d280e0314397240eb.instructions:
Preheat a charcoal or gas BBQ on high.
Grab a large bowl and add in the beef mince. Peel and finely dice the onion, then toss it in. Next, peel and finely grate the garlic straight into the bowl before adding the soy sauce, sesame oil, and honey.
Use clean hands to massage the ingredients together until well combined. Divide the mixture into eight even sized balls, 135g each. Flatten the balls into patties, a bit wider than the burger buns. Set aside between parchment paper.
Drain the excess juice off the kimchi and tip it into the mayonnaise. Run your knife through the kimchi a few times until it’s roughly chopped into small pieces. Stir the chopped kimchi into the mayonnaise until there are no streaks. Set aside until you’re ready to assemble.
Finely slice the lettuce and tomato before setting aside.
Season the patties on either side before placing them on the grill. Sear on each side for 2-3 minutes before adding a slice of cheese to each patty. Place the patties on a tray with a wire rack to allow the cheese to melt while the patties rest.
In the meantime, slice the burger buns in half and lightly toast them on the cut side until golden brown.
Once toasted, spoon a generous portion of kimchi mayonnaise on both halves of the burger bun. To the bottom bun, add the lettuce, then the tomato slices. Season the tomato with a pinch of salt. Top with the bulgogi patties and fit with the top bun before serving.

c501351c25e4e772c182d21c4081ac53c17fb463.title: One Pot Sausage and Rice
c501351c25e4e772c182d21c4081ac53c17fb463.text: This is another recipe that I like to make if I'm just making dinner for myself. Most of the ingredients I'll already have in the pantry and fridge, I'll just pick up whatever sausage I want to put with it that night. We'll only use one pan for this one so there's minimal clean up afterward. Easy Sausage and Rice DinnerWe're using a combination of base veg to build flavour, onion, garlic, carrot and celery. If you don't have celery, feel free to leave it out. Then we'll add in the chopped chorizo (or sausage of your choice) and cook it down a bit before adding our dry spices and the rice.We'll use chicken stock for the liquid to add extra flavour but you can water instead or beef/veg stock. Once it sits for a bit and soaks up most of the stock, we'll add some green (for health!) and let it sit a little longer. That's it, a very easy dinner for one person. You can up the quantities if you're cooking for more people. Ingredient NotesChorizo: Try to find a good butcher that makes chorizo sausages in your area (I like them spicy). As the fat renders from the chorizo the aromatic spices permeate throughout and give the dish a foundation of flavour. That smoky, fatty flavour is balanced by the sweetness of the vegetables and the freshness of the spinach. You can use other sausages in this recipe, just try to get one with some aromatics with the protein (Italian sausages, beef & herbs, beef & chilli, lamb & rosemary etc). Arborio rice: Arborio rice works really well in this recipe as it soaks up all of the stock without losing it's structure and texture. If you don’t have any Arborio rice on hand you can swap the Arborio for sushi rice, though you will need to use less stock. Use about 1 ½ cups of stock and check if it’s cooked after 15 minutes, as sushi rice cooks faster and requires less liquid. If you want to use a different grain altogether, pearl barley could be a good option. Keep the same weight of grain but use 650ml stock and check after 35 minutes. Pearl barley requires more liquid and takes longer to cook. Chicken stock: I never use presalted stock, no matter what I'm cooking. If I don't have time to make my own stock, I always make sure to buy unsalted chicken stock. Pre-made chicken stock is seasoned to make the stock taste right at the dilution at which it was made. When we cook with chicken stock and it reduces in volume, the salt dilution concentrates. If you’re not careful it can make the dish taste incredibly salty, before you’ve even added salt yourself.If you don’t have chicken stock, you can substitute the stock for water. The sausage and vegetables carry heaps of flavour in this recipe so you’re not missing out on too much. Another good alternative is to use a chicken stock cube diluted in 500ml instead of using real stock. Sure, you won’t get the same natural chicken flavour as you do with real stock, but it’s a good option to have. Equipment listChopping boardChef's knifeMedium-sized saucier (or a skillet, saute pan or small pot) with a lidWooden spatula or spoon
c501351c25e4e772c182d21c4081ac53c17fb463.author: Andy
c501351c25e4e772c182d21c4081ac53c17fb463.ingredients:
1 onion
1 carrot
1 stick celery
2 cloves garlic
2 chorizo sausages
2 tbsp olive oil
½ tsp smoked paprika
Salt and pepper to taste
120g (4.2 oz) Arborio rice
500ml (17 oz) chicken stock
60g (2.1 oz) baby spinach
c501351c25e4e772c182d21c4081ac53c17fb463.instructions:
Peel and finely dice the onion and carrot, finely dice the celery then set aside.
Crush and roughly chop the garlic, then set aside.
Slice the chorizo into chunks, (3-4cm thick) then set aside.
Add olive oil to a medium sized saucier. Preheat the saucier on high heat for 30 seconds.
Add the onion, carrot and celery, sweat for 2-3 minutes with ½ tsp of salt. Once the onions turn translucent, add the garlic and stir.
Add the sliced chorizo and stir into the vegetables. Cook for two minutes or until the fat begins to render out of the chorizo.
Add the smoked paprika, ¼ tsp of salt, 12 cracks of black pepper and the rice (no need to rinse the rice). Keep the saucier on the heat to lightly toast the rice for 1 minute, stir occasionally.
Add the chicken stock and stir, making sure to lift any pieces of rice stuck to the bottom of the saucier. Bring the stock to a simmer then turn the element down to low, place a lid on top and leave for 15 minutes.
Remove the lid and check the rice is soft. If the rice is still firm, place the lid back on and leave on low heat for a further 5 minutes.
Remove the lid, turn the heat up high and add the spinach. Place the lid back on for 60 seconds. Remove the lid, stir the rice and cook for a further 60 seconds.
Taste the rice and adjust seasoning if required. Plate and enjoy.

00af6dc3e2764d3552fa0c2f348b60dd24770fe1.title: A Simple Chocolate Fondant
00af6dc3e2764d3552fa0c2f348b60dd24770fe1.text: Chocolate fondant, lava cake, self-saucing pudding, whatever you call it, this is the dessert I make when I want to impress without spending all afternoon in the kitchen. It's one I made many times at a restaurant in Melbourne called Gills Diner, and I think it was the first dessert I made for Katelyn and her sister when they came to eat at the restaurant. Chocolate Fondant ExplainedThe chocolateUse good dark chocolate, 70% cocoa solids is the sweet spot. Anything less and it’ll taste like a regular chocolate sponge, anything darker and it can turn bitter. We melt the chocolate gently in a double boiler (also called a bain-marie) so the bowl doesn’t sit directly on the heat. Direct heat is the fastest way to burn or split chocolate. The steam from the simmering water below brings it up to temperature slowly and evenly. Don’t let the water touch the bottom of the bowl. The batterWhisk the eggs, egg yolks and sugar together until the mixture goes pale and ribbony. This is what gives the cake its lift, you’re whisking air into the eggs. Fold in the flour gently. Over mixing develops the gluten and the cake comes out stiff instead of soft. A pinch of salt is essential, it doesn’t taste salty, it just amplifies the chocolate flavour. The bakeThe whole trick is baking just long enough that the outside sets but the middle stays liquid. Hot oven, short time. 7 to 8 minutes at 200°C fan-forced is the sweet spot for 200ml ramekins. The top should be just set when you press it gently. Pull them out the second they look right, the residual heat keeps cooking the cakes while they sit. Run a knife around the edge after 2 minutes and invert onto plates. Ingredient NotesDark chocolate: 70% cocoa is the right balance. Use good baking chocolate, the brand you reach for matters here because the chocolate is essentially the whole flavour of the dessert. Cheap compound chocolate won’t melt the same way and the flavour will let the whole thing down. Eggs: Room temperature eggs whip up lighter and incorporate more air than cold ones. Take them out of the fridge 30 minutes before you start. The extra yolks are what give the cake its richness and help create the molten centre. Caster sugar: Caster sugar dissolves faster than regular granulated sugar when whisked into the eggs, which means a smoother batter. If you only have granulated, you can pulse it in a food processor for 10 seconds to make caster at home. EquipmentMixing bowlsHeatproof bowlSmall saucepanWhiskRubber spatulaPastry brush4 x 200ml ramekinsOven trayPallet knife or small knifeFine sieve
00af6dc3e2764d3552fa0c2f348b60dd24770fe1.author: Andy
00af6dc3e2764d3552fa0c2f348b60dd24770fe1.ingredients:
180g dark chocolate (70% cocoa)
120g unsalted butter + 10g extra for greasing
2 eggs
2 egg yolks
40g caster sugar
35g (¼ cup) plain flour
pinch of salt
icing sugar and ice cream, to serve
00af6dc3e2764d3552fa0c2f348b60dd24770fe1.instructions:
Preheat the oven to 200°C fan forced (390°F).
Break up the chocolate into small pieces and put in a heatproof bowl with the butter. Place the bowl over a saucepan of simmering water (do not allow the bottom of the bowl to touch the water) and stir until melted. Set aside for 5 minutes.
Grease 4 x 200ml capacity ramekins with the extra butter.
Whisk the eggs, egg yolks and sugar together in a large bowl until it becomes lighter in colour. Fold in the flour and salt until smooth.
Fold in the chocolate mixture until just combined, then divide the batter evenly between the ramekins.
Place on an oven tray and bake for 7-8 minutes, until the top is just set.
Remove from the oven and allow to sit for 2 minutes. Run a pallet knife around the edges of the cakes to loosen, then invert onto serving plates. Dust with some icing sugar and serve immediately with ice cream.

08eca289077d7626b9b73d21f0a6a40b9a0a3a35.title: Sticky pork rice paper rolls
08eca289077d7626b9b73d21f0a6a40b9a0a3a35.text: Rice Paper Rolls break all the rules when it comes to food on the go. Usually we think, crispy, fried and a little naughty (which I love), but this street food is light, nourishing and filled with lots of good things. They’re also very easy to make, only requiring a handful of ingredients which can be tailored to your taste. These Vietnamese rolls are something I like to make toward the end of the week when I have a few fresh vegetables in the fridge and a protein to use up. For this recipe, we’re going to make a sticky pork as the protein and that’s going to bring lots of flavour so the rest of the ingredients are just there to support. Ingredient NotesRice paper sheets: Rice paper sheets are thin, dry rounds made from rice flour. They soften quickly when dipped in water and become pliable and sticky. Find them in the Asian aisle at the supermarket or at any Asian grocery store. The key technique is to dip them briefly in cold water until just barely wet, then place them on the board. They continue to soften as you work. If they’re already completely soft when you start rolling, they’ll tear easily.Pork loin: Pork loin is lean and quick-cooking, which makes it well suited to a hot chargrill. Slice it as thinly as possible, around 3mm, so it cooks quickly and absorbs the marinade deeply. It must be fully cooled before going into the rolls, otherwise the heat softens the rice paper from the inside and makes rolling difficult.Hot honey: Hot honey is honey infused with chilli. It adds sweetness, heat and the sticky quality that helps the marinade caramelise on the chargrill. Most supermarkets stock it now, or you can make it by warming regular honey with a pinch of dried chilli flakes. If you only have regular honey, add a small extra dash of sriracha to compensate for the heat.EquipmentChopping boardChef’s knifeSaucepanChargrill pan or frying panShallow bowlTongs
08eca289077d7626b9b73d21f0a6a40b9a0a3a35.author: Andy
08eca289077d7626b9b73d21f0a6a40b9a0a3a35.ingredients:
1 tbsp sriracha
1 tbsp hot honey
1 tbsp fish sauce
1 tbsp dark soy sauce
2 cloves garlic, finely grated
350g pork loin, thinly sliced
ground white pepper, to season
100g rice vermicelli
Vietnamese mint, carrot battons, coriander, sliced spring onions for filling
peanut dipping sauce, Nuoc Cham, to serve
8 rice paper sheets
08eca289077d7626b9b73d21f0a6a40b9a0a3a35.instructions:
Combine sriracha, honey, fish sauce, soy and garlic and mix well.
Stir through pork and season with white pepper, then cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to marinate.
Cook vermicelli in a saucepan of boiling water for 1 minute, until softened. Drain and refresh under cold running water. Drain well.
Heat an oiled chargrill pan over medium-high heat.
Cook pork for 5-6 minutes, turning, until well browned and cooked through. Set aside to cool.
To assemble, dip a rice paper sheet in a shallow bowl of cold water, until just wet all over, then place smooth side down on a clean work surface.
Start layering towards the top end of the paper with Vietnamese mint, carrot, coriander, spring onions, slices of pork then vermicelli.
Fold over the top to encase the fillings, then bring in the sides and roll up to completely enclose.
Repeat with remaining ingredients, then serve immediately with dipping sauces, or store in an airtight container in the fridge.

5c6aec1175dc442004cb2bca5a221f4a4185fb68.title: Aloo paratha
5c6aec1175dc442004cb2bca5a221f4a4185fb68.text: This is an Indian flatbread stuffed with potato and it makes a great side dish to any Indian curry.
5c6aec1175dc442004cb2bca5a221f4a4185fb68.author: Andy
5c6aec1175dc442004cb2bca5a221f4a4185fb68.ingredients:
2 large potatoes, peeled and diced
360g (3 cups) of flour
1 tsp salt (for dough)
1 red onion, finely diced
thumb-sized piece of ginger, finely grated
2 green chillies, finely diced
small bunch of coriander, finely sliced
1 tsp cumin powder
1 tsp coriander powder
1 tsp garam masala
1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder
1 tsp salt (for filling)
2 tbsp ghee
5c6aec1175dc442004cb2bca5a221f4a4185fb68.instructions:
To make the dough, add the flour and salt to a bowl. Gradually add room temperature water until the dough becomes a shaggy mess. Turn it onto a floured surface and knead for 5-10 minutes until smooth, soft, and pliable. Place the dough back in the bowl, cover with a tea towel, and let it rest for 30 minutes.
For the filling, boil the potatoes in salted water until cooked through. Mash the potatoes using a ricer or hand masher, then add the remaining ingredients (except the ghee) and mix well.
Once the dough has rested, divide it into four equal pieces and roll them into tight balls. Roll each ball out into flat discs. Place an amount of potato mixture that is equal to or slightly more than the dough you started with in the centre. Bring the sides of the dough around the potato ball and close tightly.
Flip the ball so the seam is on the bottom and roll out until it's about the size of a small plate, trying not to break the dough or let the potato mixture escape.
Heat a tawa (or frying pan) over medium-high heat, add a teaspoon of ghee, and cook the flatbread until golden brown on both sides.

9585c2fb1c8cdec72a5589c4be0d4645d6423429.title: Ricotta and Silverbeet Cannelloni Ripieni
9585c2fb1c8cdec72a5589c4be0d4645d6423429.text: I really enjoy cooking with cannelloni pasta as it has a wide tubular shape which you can fill with ricotta, cheese, meats and thicker sauces. It's a shape that's not as common as others to use but I think we should all cook with it a little more. They're great for thicker or chunkier sauces. Now, different regions in Italy have different recipes for the different pasta shapes and this is the Naples version of this pasta called Cannelloni Ripieni. It's basically a spinach and ricotta stuffed cannelloni with a tomato sauce and parmesan which is oven baked. I'm swapping out the spinach for silverbeet as I think it also works really well in this dish and adds more to the flavour. It's a great dish for dinner party or even a midweek meal served with a fresh salad. Ingredient NotesSilverbeet: Silverbeet is the Australian name for chard. The variety I used has broad, dark green leaves attached to a thick white stem, and I use both parts because they each bring something different. The stems are denser and need 4 minutes to soften before the leaves go in. The leaves wilt in under 3 minutes. If you can’t find silverbeet, baby spinach works as a direct substitute. Just add the leaves whole to the oil, cook until just wilted (about 1 minute), then set aside to cool. Spinach releases more water than silverbeet, so if there’s visible pooling in the pan, drain it off before spreading out to cool.Fresh ricotta: Use full-fat fresh ricotta for this. Not the smooth, blended tub variety, you want fresh ricotta with a slight grain and some texture, which holds its structure when baked and doesn’t turn into a solid, dense mass. Fresh ricotta is available from good delis and the deli counter at larger supermarkets. If yours looks wet or watery, tip it into a fine sieve lined with a paper towel and let it drain for 20 to 30 minutes before using. Excess moisture in the filling will make the pasta soft and soggy after baking.Fresh nutmeg: Freshly grated nutmeg has a warm, slightly sweet and almost piney aroma that pre-ground nutmeg loses quickly after milling. In a ricotta filling, it does important seasoning work, cutting through the richness of the dairy and lifting the greens. Use a Microplane or the fine side of a box grater and grate directly over the pan. A quarter of a whole nutmeg is roughly what you’re after. If you only have ground nutmeg, start with a small pinch and taste as you go. EquipmentChopping boardChef’s knife2 large saucepansLarge mixing bowlMicroplane or fine graterPiping bag24cm square baking dishAluminium foil
9585c2fb1c8cdec72a5589c4be0d4645d6423429.author: Andy
9585c2fb1c8cdec72a5589c4be0d4645d6423429.ingredients:
250g dried cannelloni shells
1 tbsp olive oil
2 cloves garlic, smashed
700ml passata
1 sprig basil
150g mozzarella, thinly sliced
1 small bunch silverbeet (approx 500g) or baby spinach
1 tbsp olive oil
300g fresh ricotta
50g parmesan cheese, finely grated
fresh nutmeg
sea salt and black pepper
9585c2fb1c8cdec72a5589c4be0d4645d6423429.instructions:
Trim the greens from the white stems of the silverbeet. Finely dice the stems and roughly chop the leaves.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan on medium heat. Add the silverbeet stems and cook for 4 minutes, until softened. Stir in the leaves, some freshly grated nutmeg (¼), a pinch of salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Continue cooking until just wilted (max 3 minutes). Remove from the heat, spread out on a tray and allow to cool (can place in the fridge to cool down faster).
In a bowl, break up the ricotta and then add parmesan, small pinch of salt and a little more grated nutmeg.
Mix in the silverbeet, then check your seasoning.
Heat the oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the garlic cloves and allow to infuse the oil for 2 minutes.
Pour in the passatta, then add a little water to the jar to mix with the remaining sauce and pour in too. Stir to combine, season with salt and add the basil. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes.
Transfer ricotta filling to a piping bag and snip the end large enough to fit inside the cannelloni shells. Pipe the filling into the shells from end to end. Use both ends to fill the cannelloni by aiming for the centre and piping outwards on both sides.
Spoon some of the tomato sauce into the base of a 24cm square baking dish (2.6qt capacity) and spread to just cover the base. Leave the whole garlic behind, you don’t need it anymore.
Place in the cannelloni shells, fitting snugly side by side in a single layer. Pour over the remaining sauce.
Top with the mozzarella slices then loosely cover the dish with foil.
Preheat the oven to 180°C fan forced (355°F). Bake the cannelloni for 25 minutes, then uncover and bake a further 10-15 minutes, until the cheese is golden.
Allow to cool for 5 minutes, then serve cannelloni garnished with some extra basil, or a side salad if you like.

c72c913fbb3e922870491f22956bcef887741b21.title: Oxtail Agnolotti
c72c913fbb3e922870491f22956bcef887741b21.text: Rich, slow-braised oxtail wrapped in homemade pasta and served with a silky sauce made from the braising liquid itself.Katelyn loves it when I make her fresh pasta, but it does take time, so I save it for special occasions. This dish has a few steps: you’re braising the oxtail low and slow until it falls apart, making a simple pasta dough from scratch, shaping it around the filling, and turning the leftover braising liquid into the sauce. It sounds like a lot, but none of it is difficult. It just takes patience.The result is a plate of pasta that genuinely tastes like something you’d get at a great restaurant, and that moment of putting it on the table makes every bit of the effort worth it. Ingredient Notes‘00’ flour: This is a very finely milled Italian flour made specifically for pasta. It creates a smooth, silky dough that rolls out beautifully and gives the pasta a great texture. You can find it in most supermarkets or Italian grocery stores. Regular plain flour will work, but the texture won’t be quite as good.Oxtail: This is the tail of a cow, cut into sections. It has a rich, deep beefy flavour and a lot of tough tissue that, once cooked slowly over several hours, melts into the sauce and makes it wonderfully thick and sticky. You can get it from a butcher, either whole or already cut into portions. If you can’t find it, osso bucco, chuck steak or oyster blade are all good alternatives.Beef tallow: This is rendered beef fat and it’s great for searing because it can handle very high heat and adds a rich flavour to the meat. You can find it at most butchers or online. If you don’t have it, any neutral oil works perfectly well.Red wine: The wine you use will influence the flavour of the whole dish, so use something you’d actually enjoy drinking. Italian reds like Barolo, Barbaresco or Nebbiolo work really well, but Merlot or Cabernet Sauvignon are great options too. Avoid anything labelled “cooking wine” as these are usually poor quality.Fine semolina: Used to dust the tray where your finished agnolotti rest before cooking. It prevents them from sticking much better than flour, because it doesn’t absorb moisture the same way.Equipment you’ll needLarge heavy-based saucepan or Dutch oven with a lidPasta machineLarge saucepan (for cooking the pasta)Chopping board and knifeBench scraperCrimped pastry wheel or sharp knifeFine sieve or strainerSlotted spoonLarge tray
c72c913fbb3e922870491f22956bcef887741b21.author: Andy
c72c913fbb3e922870491f22956bcef887741b21.ingredients:
200g ‘00’ flour, plus extra for dusting
2 eggs
10ml extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt, to season
2 tbsp fine semolina, for dusting
1kg (2.2 Lbs) oxtail
1 tbsp beef tallow (or neutral flavoured oil)
½ brown onion
1 carrot
1 stick celery
3 cloves garlic
2 sprigs rosemary
2 tbsp tomato paste
200mls red wine
1L beef stock
grated parmesan cheese, to serve
c72c913fbb3e922870491f22956bcef887741b21.instructions:
Season the oxtail on all sides with salt on a large tray.
Heat the tallow in a large, heavy based saucepan or dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the oxtail and cook for 6-8 minutes, turning until browned all over. Set aside in a bowl.
Roughly chop the carrots, onion and celery. Add the onions and carrots to the pan and cook for 3 minutes, to soften.
Add the celery and garlic and stir constantly to avoid the garlic catching and burning. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the tomato paste, stirring for 1 minute.
Add the red wine and bring to a simmer, then cook until the wine reduces by half.
Return the oxtail to the pan with the rosemary and pour in the beef stock. Cover with a lid and simmer for 4 hours, until fall apart tender (start checking for tenderness at 3 hours of cooking).
Place the flour on a clean work surface and make a well in the center. Crack the eggs into the center and season with a pinch of salt.
Add the olive oil and using a fork, whisk from the middle outside until you reach a clumpy dough, then use a bench scraper to bring it together. Knead for 4-5 minutes, or until the dough is nice and smooth.
Cover the dough in plastic wrap or in a ziplock bag. Set aside in the fridge to rest for a minimum 2 hours, ideally up to 24 hours.
Remove the oxtail from the pan and pass the sauce through a sieve to remove the aromatics. Return the sauce to the pan with the oxtail and leave to cool, covered, for at least 1 hour.
Remove the oxtail from the stock and place in a large bowl. Place the stock back over a medium heat. Bring to a boil and cook until the liquid reduces and thickens slightly.
Pick the meat from the bones, discarding the bones and any excess hard fat. Shred the meat really finely using your hands.
Stir through a little of the reduced stock to keep it moist if it needs it. Set aside to cool.
Divide the pasta dough in half and keep one covered while you work with the first. Roll the dough through a pasta machine on the biggest setting twice. Do an envelope fold on the sheet and press down to seal with your hands, then return to the pasta machine on the same setting. Roll it through twice more.
Turn the pasta machine setting down 1 notch, then pass the dough through twice. Continue to do this through each setting, until you have a long, thin pasta sheet (only use flour to dust the machine when necessary to avoid sticking).
Cut the pasta sheet in half to make 2 long even sheets and place on a lightly floured bench.
Add tablespoonfuls of the oxtail filling along the closest edge to you, evenly spaced, with a 1cm gap in between. Brush the far edge with a little water.
Fold over the far edge to enclose the filling and press down along the seam, then in between each portion of filling.
Cut the long edge with a crimped dough roller to make a straight edge. Then roll the Agnolotti over the long edge and use the roller to cut between them. Make sure each agnolotti is sealed.
Transfer the pieces to a tray sprinkled with semolina. Refrigerate, uncovered, until ready to cook.
Bring a large saucepan of salted water to the boil over high heat. Add the agnolotti and cook for 6 minutes, until the dough is tender and al dente.
Using a slotted spoon, transfer the cooked pasta straight into the reduced sauce and toss gently to combine. Divide the pasta between serving plates and sprinkle with some grated parmesan cheese to serve.

e5202a456caababcd9f8bd2cfd3fecf75fc8e748.title: Lu rou fan
e5202a456caababcd9f8bd2cfd3fecf75fc8e748.text: Lu Rou Fan, haven’t heard of it? Well, it’s a delicious Taiwanese dish made with braised pork belly, fragrant rice, boiled eggs and bok choy. It does take a couple of hours to make, so it’s great for when you’re having a slow day.
e5202a456caababcd9f8bd2cfd3fecf75fc8e748.author: Andy
e5202a456caababcd9f8bd2cfd3fecf75fc8e748.ingredients:
1 kg (2.2 lbs) of skin-on pork belly, diced into 1 cm (0.4 inch) cubes
2 tbsp peanut oil
4 shallots, sliced thinly
4 eggs, hard-boiled for 8 minutes
8 slices of ginger
8 cloves of garlic, peeled
1 star anise
1 cinnamon stick
3 bay leaves
3 tbsp of rock sugar
7 tbsp of light soy sauce
1 cup (240 ml) of Shaoxing wine
1 tbsp of dark soy sauce
1 tsp of white pepper
1 tsp of five-spice powder
2 cups (475 ml) of water
Steamed rice and bok choy to serve
e5202a456caababcd9f8bd2cfd3fecf75fc8e748.instructions:
Place a pot, for which you have a lid, over medium heat. Add the oil and diced pork. Cook over medium heat to start rendering the fat and to begin browning. This will take around 30 minutes.
Remove most of the pork fat from the pot, reserving it to fry the shallots.
To the pork, add the ginger, garlic, cinnamon stick, star anise, bay leaves, Shaoxing wine, rock sugar, light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, white pepper, and five-spice powder.
Turn the heat back to medium and stir well. Then add the water, give it one last stir, bring to a light simmer, and cover with the lid. Reduce heat to low and cook for 1.5 hours.
While the pork is simmering, add the rendered pork fat to a small pot and fry the shallots until golden brown (if you don't have enough pork fat, you can add some oil). Once golden brown, remove and set aside.
After the pork has cooked for 30 minutes, add the fried shallots and peeled boiled eggs. Continue cooking for the remaining hour.
At the one-hour mark, remove the lid to allow the sauce to thicken slightly.
Once cooked, remove any aromatics and serve on steamed rice with steamed bok choy on the side.

ef36207cac8f792a5f6e53cd8b6f361769679960.title: Hoisin and Chilli Pork
ef36207cac8f792a5f6e53cd8b6f361769679960.text: This is one of the easiest (and cheapest) stir fry sauce and I think it rivals your favourite Chinese restaurant. This is a velveted pork stir-fry built around hoisin and fresh chilli. Velveting is a Chinese technique where the protein is coated in a small amount of cornflour before it hits the wok: the starch forms a thin protective layer around the pork that stays tender even on very high heat. Hoisin sauce is a thick, fermented soybean-based condiment with a deep, slightly sweet savouriness that clings to the meat and vegetables and reduces quickly at wok temperature. The Shaoxing wine and soy marinade penetrates the pork and adds a base layer of seasoning before the cook even starts.The entire cook from wok on to plate is about 10 minutes, so everything needs to be prepped and ready before you start. You need to make sure your wok is night and hot before you start. A wok that isn’t hot enough will steam the pork instead of searing it, giving you grey, soft meat rather than a browned crust. Cook the pork in batches to keep the wok temperature up, set it aside, then build the vegetable base and sauce in the same wok before everything comes back together at the end. The sesame oil goes in just before the heat goes off. It’s a finishing oil, not a cooking one, and it loses its aroma quickly if added too early.Ingredient NotesCornflour: The cornflour in this marinade is doing the work of velveting. Tossing the pork slices in cornflour before adding the wet marinade coats the surface of the meat with a thin layer of starch. On contact with the hot wok, that coat sets into a tender, lightly textured exterior that stays moist even under aggressive heat. Without it, sliced pork fillet in a hot wok will tighten, release moisture, and may come out dry.Hoisin sauce: Hoisin is a thick, dark, sweet-savoury Chinese condiment made from fermented soybeans, garlic, and spices. It’s not the same as oyster sauce or black bean sauce: it’s sweeter and more pungent, and it coats ingredients well because of its thick consistency. Different brands vary in sweetness and saltiness, so taste the dish before adding any extra seasoning at the end.Shaoxing wine: Shaoxing is a Chinese rice wine used widely in marinades and stir-fries. In this recipe it’s in the pork marinade, where it adds depth and helps the cornflour adhere. It has a warm, slightly nutty flavour and is available in the Asian section of most supermarkets or at Asian grocers. If you can’t find it, dry sherry is a reasonable substitute.EquipmentChopping boardChef’s knifeWok or large frying panWok spatula or tongsLarge bowl (for marinating)Grater or microplaneLadle or large spoon
ef36207cac8f792a5f6e53cd8b6f361769679960.author: Andy
ef36207cac8f792a5f6e53cd8b6f361769679960.ingredients:
500g pork fillet, thinly sliced
1 tsp cornflour (cornstarch)
1 tsp Shaoxing (Chinese cooking wine)
2 tsp light soy sauce
2 tbsp neutral oil (peanut/ canola/ vegetable)
1 red onion, thinly sliced
thumb-size piece fresh ginger, finely grated
4 cloves garlic, finely grated
1-2 long red chillies, thinly sliced
2 zucchini, sliced .5 cm think
2 tbsp Hoisin sauce
1 tbsp fish sauce
1 tsp sesame oil
steamed rice, to serve
ef36207cac8f792a5f6e53cd8b6f361769679960.instructions:
Place the pork in a large bowl, add the cornflour and toss well to coat.
Stir through the Shaoxing and soy sauce, then marinate for 10 minutes to 1 hour.
Heat half the oil in a wok over high heat.
Sear the pork in batches, until just browned, then set aside.
Heat the remaining oil in the wok over high heat.
Add the onion, cook for 1 minute, tossing.
Stir in ginger, garlic and chillies, cook for 30 seconds, stirring.
Add the zucchini and cook until starting to soften.
Return the pork to the wok and stir in the hoisin and fish sauce. Toss well to combine.
Finish with a drizzle of sesame oil and remove from the heat.
Serve immediately with steamed rice.

e957d1e5be0547ed29519700099351811fd7a105.title: Peanut Butter Ramen
e957d1e5be0547ed29519700099351811fd7a105.text: My go-to late night dinner after working a busy shift in a kitchen. This is a 5-minute ramen that uses the seasoning sachets from a packet of Shin Ramen Black as the broth base. All the packets go in: powder, oil, dried vegetables, which gives you a well-seasoned, spiced broth without having to build one from scratch. Peanut butter goes in with the seasoning before the noodles, so it has time to melt into the liquid and emulsify with the broth. It adds fat and body without making it taste noticeably of peanuts. The egg is beaten and stirred in gradually while the broth is still moving, which distributes it in fine strands through the liquid rather than setting it in clumps.The recipe uses 500ml of water, which is less than the packet instructions suggest. Less water means a more concentrated broth, richer and more intensely seasoned. Pre-cooked chicken goes in with the noodles so it just needs to warm through. The whole cook is about 5 minutes from cold water. I eat this after a long service when I want something hot and savoury without much effort. It scales up easily if you have multiple pots going at once.Ingredient NotesShin Ramen Black: Shin Ramen Black is a Korean instant noodle that comes with three seasoning sachets: a powder packet, a flavoured oil packet, and a dried vegetable and meat packet. It has a higher spice level and more depth than standard instant ramen, and that intensity works well against the peanut butter. Any instant ramen brand works as a substitute, but the flavour of the finished dish will be milder. Look for it in Asian supermarkets or the international aisle of larger supermarkets.Crunchy peanut butter: Crunchy peanut butter adds both fat and texture. It melts into the hot broth and emulsifies with the liquid, adding body to the broth without thickening it noticeably. The peanut pieces give a small amount of crunch against the soft noodles. Smooth peanut butter works fine if that’s what you have, but you lose the textural contrast. One tablespoon in 500ml of broth is enough to taste it without it dominating. Natural peanut butters can separate in hot liquid, so stir the jar well before measuring.Chilli crisp: Chilli crisp (also sold as chilli oil with crispy bits) is a finishing condiment, not a cooking ingredient in this recipe. The oil carries heat and flavour, and the crispy fried aromatics in the jar add texture and a roasted, slightly smoky note. Lao Gan Ma is the most widely available brand in Australia. Start with a teaspoon and add more to taste. The Shin Ramen Black seasoning is already spiced, so the total heat level builds quickly.EquipmentSmall saucepanSmall bowl (for beating egg)ForkChopping boardChef’s knifeWooden spoon or chopsticksServing bowl
e957d1e5be0547ed29519700099351811fd7a105.author: Andy
e957d1e5be0547ed29519700099351811fd7a105.ingredients:
130g pkt Shin Ramen Black
½ cup cooked chicken, shredded
1 tbsp crunchy peanut butter
2 eggs, beaten
1 spring onion, sliced, white and green parts separated
chilli crisp, to serve
e957d1e5be0547ed29519700099351811fd7a105.instructions:
Place 500ml water in a small saucepan over medium heat.
Empty all the seasoning packets from the ramen noodles packet into the water along with the peanut butter. Stir to combine until water comes to a simmer.
Add noodles and cook for 45 seconds, then stir to break up the noodles a little. Stir in the chicken and spring onion whites.
Gradually add the egg, stirring constantly until incorporated then take off the heat.
Stir through half of the spring onion greens, then transfer to a serving bowl. Garnish with remaining spring onion and drizzle with some chilli crisp.

7eeb3d4a4a508dac6e2ba835cd34df241d516cc3.title: Southern Style Black Eyed Peas
7eeb3d4a4a508dac6e2ba835cd34df241d516cc3.text: This is my take on a Southern staple that I keep coming back to. It’s built on a base of smoked bacon, chorizo and the holy trinity of capsicum, celery and onion, then simmered with black eyed peas in chicken stock until everything is thick and deeply flavoured. The finish is a quick pulse with a stick blender to puree about a third of the peas, which gives it a creamy texture without losing all the bite. It’s a one-pot dish and it reheats well all week. Black eyed peas are traditionally eaten on New Year’s Day in the Southern US for good luck and prosperity, and I’ve kept the spirit of the dish while streamlining the process so it comes together in under an hour once the peas are soaked. The soaking step is non-negotiable: at least 3 hours but overnight is better. After that the cooking is straightforward. I use beef bacon here but smoked pork bacon or speck both work well in its place. Ingredient NotesBlack eyed peas: Also known as cowpeas, black eyed peas are a legume rather than a true pea. I use dried rather than canned for this recipe as they hold their shape better during the simmer and absorb more flavour from the stock. Soak them for at least 3 hours, but overnight gives the best result. Drain and rinse well before adding to the pot. If you’re short on time, canned will work but reduce the simmering time by about half. Smoked chorizo: The chorizo brings fat, smoke and a deep paprika flavour that sets the tone for the whole dish. I use a smoked, cured variety rather than fresh, which has a firmer texture and more concentrated flavour. Kielbasa is a good substitute, or andouille if you want a spicier result. The sausage is browned first so it renders some fat into the base before the vegetables go in. Smoked paprika: It does a lot of work here alongside the spice blend and the chorizo. I use sweet smoked paprika rather than hot as the cayenne is already handling the heat. Buy a fresh tin if yours has been sitting in the pantry for more than six months as paprika loses its intensity quickly, and a stale tin will flatten the whole dish. EquipmentChopping boardChef’s knifeLarge heavy-based saucepan with lidWooden spoonStick blender (immersion blender)Large container (for soaking the peas)Ladle
7eeb3d4a4a508dac6e2ba835cd34df241d516cc3.author: Andy
7eeb3d4a4a508dac6e2ba835cd34df241d516cc3.ingredients:
300g (1½ cups) black eyed peas
1 tbsp olive oil
200g smoked bacon (beef bacon), diced
1 smoked chorizo sausage (or kielbasa), diced
1 red capsicum (bell pepper), diced
1 green capsicum (bell pepper), diced
1 celery stick, diced
2 spring onions, sliced, white and green parts separated
1 brown onion, diced
5 cloves garlic, diced
3 fresh bay leaves
1 tsp dried oregano
1½ tsp smoked paprika
1 tsp cayenne pepper
1 tsp garlic powder
1 tsp onion powder
1 L chicken stock
⅓ cup flat leaf parsley, finely chopped
7eeb3d4a4a508dac6e2ba835cd34df241d516cc3.instructions:
Rinse the black eye peas under cold water and discard any broken ones.
Place the peas in a large container and cover with plenty of water. Cover and set aside to soak for 3-4 hours, but ideally overnight.
Dice the bacon, chorizo, capsicums, celery, brown onion and garlic. Slice the spring onions and separate the green and white parts.
Heat the oil in a large heavy based saucepan over medium high heat.
Cook the bacon for 2-3 minutes, until the fat has rendered and it starts to brown.
Add the sausage and cook, stirring occasionally, for a further few minutes.
Add the capsicums, celery, brown onion, garlic and spring onion whites to the pan. Cook for 8-10 minutes until starting to soften, stirring often.
Add the bay leaves, dried oregano, smoked paprika, cayenne, garlic powder and onion powder. Stir well to combine and cook until the spices are fragrant.
Mix in the drained peas and the stock. Bring to a simmer, then cover with a lid and reduce the heat to medium low.
Simmer for 15 minutes, then uncover and cook for a further 10 minutes.
Turn the heat off and remove the bay leaves. Using a stick blender(immersion blender), pulse the soup a little to puree one third of the peas. Stir through the spring onion greens and fresh parsley, and serve!

1ffe8f849c9c253fb5a483d16517c53978585b81.title: The reuben
1ffe8f849c9c253fb5a483d16517c53978585b81.text: The reuben is a deli classic that layers succulent corned beef, tangy sauerkraut, melting Swiss cheese, and creamy Russian dressing between slices of crisp rye bread. This recipe promises an epic mix of flavours and textures, making it a must-try for sandwich lovers! Perfect for a satisfying lunch or a comforting dinner, so try making it at home next time you're craving a sandwich.
1ffe8f849c9c253fb5a483d16517c53978585b81.author: Andy
1ffe8f849c9c253fb5a483d16517c53978585b81.ingredients:
800g (28 oz) cooked corned beef, sliced about 0.5cm (1/5 inch) thick
1 loaf of rye bread, sliced around 1cm (2/5 inch) thick on the angle
5 tbsp mayonnaise
2 tbsp ketchup
1 tbsp gherkin relish
1 shallot, finely grated
4 dashes Worcestershire sauce
16 slices Swiss cheese
half of a 500g (17.6 oz) jar of sauerkraut, squeezed to remove excess moisture
1ffe8f849c9c253fb5a483d16517c53978585b81.instructions:
In a bowl, mix together the mayonnaise, ketchup, gherkin relish, grated shallot, and Worcestershire sauce until well combined.
Heat a grill or skillet over medium heat. Grill the slices of rye bread on both sides until lightly toasted. Briefly grill the slices of corned beef to warm them up.
Spread a generous amount of the Thousand Island dressing on both sides of the toasted rye bread. On one slice, layer the warmed corned beef, followed by the squeezed sauerkraut, and top with Swiss cheese slices.
Place the open-faced sandwich under a grill or in a broiler, cheese side up, until the cheese is melted and gooey. Cover with the other slice of bread, press down gently, slice in half, and serve warm.

41de4bff4035b72d69c2bab987621d9c522ef304.title: Simple Chicken Curry
41de4bff4035b72d69c2bab987621d9c522ef304.text: This is the kind of curry I throw together on a weeknight when I want something hearty but don’t have time for a 3-hour braise. It’s not from any one place, it's just something I built using what i had in the pantry and fridge. Simple ingredients, easy steps to follow and a tasty curry after 40 minutes. My Chicken Curry ExplainedBuilding the baseEvery good curry starts with toasting whole spices in hot oil before anything else goes in. We use cinnamon stick and green cardamom pods here, both of which release their oils into the cooking fat and flavour everything that follows. Once they’re fragrant, the sliced onions go in with a pinch of salt and cook down until they’re properly golden. Don’t rush this step. The colour you get on the onions is the colour and depth you get in the finished sauce. The chicken and dry spicesWe're using chicken thigh so it stays juicy through the simmer and has more flavour than breast. Cut into bite-sized pieces, the chicken goes in after the onions and gets stirred through, then the dry spices (cumin, garam masala, Kashmiri chilli) hit the pan along with the grated garlic and ginger. We toast everything briefly in the fat for a minute before adding water to deglaze and lift the fond off the bottom of the pan. The fond is concentrated flavour, don’t leave it behind. The simmerTinned tomatoes go in next, water swilled through the tin so nothing is wasted. Drop the heat to low and let the curry simmer gently for 5 to 7 minutes. The sauce will start to thicken and the chicken finishes cooking through. Asparagus goes in at the end for a 2 minute simmer so it stays bright green and crisp-tender. Ingredient NotesChicken thighs: Boneless, skinless thigh is the cut for this curry. It stays moist and tender through the simmer where chicken breast would dry out. Cut into bite-sized pieces (around 1cm x 4cm strips) so it cooks quickly and the sauce has plenty of surface area to cling to. Kashmiri chilli powder: This is what gives the curry its deep red colour without adding aggressive heat. The 0.5 to 2 tsp range lets you dial the spice level to your taste. If you can’t find Kashmiri, swap in regular chilli powder at half the amount and add a teaspoon of paprika for the colour. Whole spices: Cinnamon stick and cardamom pods release more flavour than the ground versions, and they’re essential to the base of this curry. Fish them out at the end if you don’t want anyone biting into a whole cardamom pod, or leave them in and warn everyone at the table. EquipmentChopping boardChef’s knifeMicroplane or fine graterHeavy-based pot with lidWooden spoonSmall saucepan
41de4bff4035b72d69c2bab987621d9c522ef304.author: Andy
41de4bff4035b72d69c2bab987621d9c522ef304.ingredients:
Basmati rice to serve (1 cup rice + 1.5 cups water)
2 brown onions, sliced thin
3cm piece ginger, finely grated
5 cloves garlic, finely grated
2 bunches asparagus, sliced into 5cm pieces
600g thigh fillets, cut into 1cm x 4 cm
